The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then $F$ is differentiable for almost every $x\in(a,b)$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)$$
at every such point.

Let $(K,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space. Every member of
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is bounded, so the supremum metric

$$d_\infty(f,g):=\sup_{x\in K}|f(x)-g(x)|$$

is defined on $C(K,\mathbb{R})$. With this metric,
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is complete.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For any Lebesgue-integrable vector function $h$ with $\int\|h\|_2<\infty$, write $I=\int h$. If $I=0$, the norm inequality is immediate. Otherwise put $q=I/\|I\|_2$. Then $\|I\|_2=\int q^Th\le\int|q^Th|\le\int\|h\|_2$, by [F1], linearity componentwise, and $\|q\|_2=1$. Thus the vector integral estimate needed below holds for these Lebesgue integrands. Now put $g=Bu\in L^1(0,T;\mathbb R^n)$; this follows from $B\in L^\infty$, $u\in L^2$, and [F5]. Choose a finite partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$ with $\|A\|_\infty(t_{j+1}-t_j)<1$ on each subinterval when $\|A\|_\infty>0$; if $\|A\|_\infty=0$, use $N=1$. Given the already constructed value $x(t_j)$, define $\mathcal T z(t)=x(t_j)+\int_{t_j}^t(A(s)z(s)+g(s))ds$ on $C([t_j,t_{j+1}];\mathbb R^n)$. By [F2], $\mathcal T$ maps continuous functions to continuous functions, and the vector-integral estimate just proved gives $\|\mathcal T z-\mathcal T w\|_\infty\le q_j\|z-w\|_\infty$ with $q_j=\|A\|_\infty(t_{j+1}-t_j)<1$.

Starting from the constant function $z_0=x(t_j)$, let $z_{k+1}=\mathcal T z_k$. Then $\|z_{k+1}-z_k\|_\infty\le q_j^k\|z_1-z_0\|_\infty$, so the successive differences have summable norms. Each coordinate converges uniformly by [F3], and the finite coordinate limit is a continuous vector function $z$. The integral estimate in step 1.1 makes $\mathcal T$ continuous in the supremum norm, hence $z=\mathcal Tz$. If $z,w$ are two fixed points, $\|z-w\|_\infty\le q_j\|z-w\|_\infty$, so $z=w$. Solving the finitely many subintervals in order gives one continuous solution on $[0,T]$, and the same uniqueness on each subinterval proves global uniqueness.

The integrand $Ax+Bu$ lies in $L^1$. Its indefinite integral is absolutely continuous by [F2], as required in the Statement. Under [A1], the $L^1$ fundamental theorem in [F2] differentiates the integral equation almost everywhere and yields $\dot x=Ax+Bu$. The same equation is independent of the chosen representatives of $A,B,u$ by [F6].

From the integral equation and step 1.1, $\|x(t)\|_2\le \|x_0\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\|u\|_{L^1}+\|A\|_\infty\int_0^t\|x(s)\|_2ds$. Apply [F4] with $c=\|x_0\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\|u\|_{L^1}$ and then [F5]; this gives the displayed supremum bound.

Linearity of the integral [F6] shows that a linear combination of two zero-initial-state solutions is the solution for the same linear combination of controls; uniqueness from step 2.1 makes the zero-initial-state map linear. Step 3.2 with $x_0=0$ bounds this linear map in the $L^2$ and supremum norms, while the fixed initial-state contribution is independent of $u$. Hence the full map is affine and bounded as claimed.

Let $U_c\subset\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, compact and convex. The pointwise control set is
$$
\mathcal U_c:=\{u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m):u(t)\in U_c\text{ for almost every }t\}.

Let $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite. For each $u\in\mathcal U_c$, its state is the unique continuous solution of the Volterra equation
$$
x_u(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x_u(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
The same state equation is defined for every $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and the running and terminal cost on that ambient space is
$$
J(u)=\frac12\int_0^T\!\left((x_u(t)-x_d(t))^TQ(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t))+u(t)^TR(t)u(t)\right)dt+\frac12(x_u(T)-x_T)^TP(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$

derivations.claim: For $q\in\mathbb R^m$ set $h(q)=\sup_{c\in U_c}q^Tc$, which is finite because $U_c$ is compact and hence bounded. If $z\notin U_c$, [F3] gives a nearest point $y\in U_c$ to $z$. For each $c\in U_c$ and $0<\theta\le1$, convexity gives $y+\theta(c-y)\in U_c$; minimality of $y$ implies $\|z-y-\theta(c-y)\|_2^2\ge\|z-y\|_2^2$, and division by $\theta$ followed by $\theta\downarrow0$ gives $(z-y)^T(c-y)\le0$. Thus $q_0=z-y$ satisfies $q_0^Tz-h(q_0)\ge\|z-y\|_2^2>0$. If $M_c=\sup_{c\in U_c}\|c\|_2$, then $|h(q)-h(q_0)|\le M_c\|q-q_0\|_2$ and $|(q-q_0)^Tz|\le\|q-q_0\|_2\|z\|_2$. Rational vectors are dense in $\mathbb R^m$, so one can choose rational $q$ close enough to $q_0$ that $q^Tz>h(q)$. Therefore a point $z$ belongs to $U_c$ exactly when $q^Tz\le h(q)$ for every rational vector $q$.

Fix a rational $q$. Every $u_k$ is in $\mathcal U_c$, so $h(q)-q^Tu_k(t)\ge0$ almost everywhere. For any measurable $E\subseteq[0,T]$, the test function $q\mathbf1_E$ lies in $L^2$ because $T<\infty$; weak convergence, [F2], and [F4] give $\int_Eq^Tu\,dt=\lim_k\int_Eq^Tu_k\,dt\le h(q)|E|$. If $q^Tu>h(q)$ on a set of positive measure, then for some integer $r\ge1$ the measurable set $E_r=\{t:q^Tu(t)\ge h(q)+1/r\}$ has positive measure, contradicting the integral inequality with $E=E_r$. Hence $q^Tu(t)\le h(q)$ almost everywhere.

The rational vectors form a countable set, so the exceptional null sets from step 1.2 have a null union. Outside that union all rational support inequalities hold simultaneously; step 1.1 then gives $u(t)\in U_c$ almost everywhere. This is exactly $u\in\mathcal U_c$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. Finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
boxes are dense in $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, state and control dimensions $n,m\ge1$, and the real quotient space $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$ of measurable controls modulo equality almost everywhere ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Let $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$ be equivalence classes, let $x_0,x_T\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $x_d\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^n)$. Let $U_c\subset\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, compact and convex. The pointwise control set is
$$
\mathcal U_c:=\{u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m):u(t)\in U_c\text{ for almost every }t\}.
$$
Let $Q\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $R\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{m\times m})$ be symmetric almost everywhere, with $Q(t)\succeq0$ and $rI\preceq R(t)\preceq MI$ almost everywhere for constants $0<r\le M<\infty$. Let $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite. For each $u\in\mathcal U_c$, its state is the unique continuous solution of the Volterra equation
$$
x_u(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x_u(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
The same state equation is defined for every $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and the running and terminal cost on that ambient space is
$$
J(u)=\frac12\int_0^T\!\left((x_u(t)-x_d(t))^TQ(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t))+u(t)^TR(t)u(t)\right)dt+\frac12(x_u(T)-x_T)^TP(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$
The constrained problem minimizes this ambient functional over $\mathcal F$, where additional path or terminal constraints are represented by a nonempty convex weakly sequentially closed set $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal U_c$; with no additional state constraints, $\mathcal F=\mathcal U_c$. “Weakly sequentially closed” means that every weakly convergent sequence in $\mathcal F$ has its weak limit in $\mathcal F$ ([[def-weak-convergence-of-nets-and-sequences]]). The definition asserts no optimizer or adjoint existence; the state-map well-definedness is supplied by [[lem-ctrl1-measurable-linear-ode-state-map]].
For the data of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]], if $u_k,u\in\mathcal U_c$ and $u_k\rightharpoonup u$ weakly in $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, then $x_{u_k}\to x_u$ uniformly on $[0,T]$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$

are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $U_c\subset\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, compact and convex, and let $\mathcal U_c$ be the pointwise admissible set in [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]]. If $u_k\in\mathcal U_c$ and $u_k\rightharpoonup u$ weakly in real $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, then $u\in\mathcal U_c$. Thus $\mathcal U_c$ is weakly sequentially closed.

derivations.claim: By [F4], the weak limit $u$ belongs to $\mathcal U_c$, so [F2] applies. Put $e_k=x_{u_k}-x_d$ and $e=x_u-x_d$; their difference $e_k-e=x_{u_k}-x_u$ tends to zero uniformly. Since $Q$ is essentially bounded, the estimate $|a^TQ(t)a-b^TQ(t)b|\le\|Q(t)\|_2(\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2)\|a-b\|_2$ shows that $\int_0^T e_k^TQe_k\,dt\to\int_0^T e^TQe\,dt$. The terminal terms converge by the same estimate with $P$ and $x_{u_k}(T)\to x_u(T)$.

Let $\mathscr Rv=R(\cdot)v(\cdot)$. The bounds on $R$ imply $\|\mathscr Rv\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ and $\langle\mathscr Rv,v\rangle\ge0$; symmetry gives $\langle\mathscr Rv,w\rangle=\langle v,\mathscr Rw\rangle$. For every fixed $w\in L^2$, $\langle\mathscr Ru_k,u_k\rangle\ge2\langle\mathscr Ru_k,w\rangle-\langle\mathscr Rw,w\rangle$, because the difference is $\langle\mathscr R(u_k-w),u_k-w\rangle\ge0$. The right-hand side converges to $2\langle\mathscr Ru,w\rangle-\langle\mathscr Rw,w\rangle$ by weak convergence, as [F3] makes $v\mapsto\langle\mathscr Rv,w\rangle=\langle v,\mathscr Rw\rangle$ bounded. The state and terminal cost terms converge by step 1.1, while the control quadratic term is lower semicontinuous by step 1.2. Multiplying by $1/2$ and adding these three terms gives $J(u)\le\liminf_k J(u_k)$.

Let $T>0$, $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$, $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$, $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$. Write $\|A\|_\infty$ and $\|B\|_\infty$ for the essential suprema of their Euclidean operator norms. There is a unique absolutely continuous $x:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n$ satisfying
$$
x(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
Under Countable Choice it satisfies $\dot x=A x+B u$ almost everywhere, and it always satisfies
$$
\|x\|_\infty\le e^{\|A\|_\infty T}\left(\|x_0\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\sqrt T\,\|u\|_2\right).
$$
For fixed $A,B,x_0$, the map $u\mapsto x_u$ is affine into $C([0,T];\mathbb R^n)$, and its zero-initial-state linear part is bounded from $L^2$ to the supremum norm.

The almost-everywhere derivative assertion uses Countable Choice, as required by the cited $L^1$ fundamental theorem. The integral-equation existence, uniqueness, bound, and affine-map claims do not require that axiom.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For the data of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]] and an admissible control $u$ with state $x_u$, a **continuous LQR adjoint** is an absolutely continuous curve $p:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n$ satisfying, almost everywhere,
$$
-\dot p(t)=A(t)^Tp(t)+Q(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t)),\qquad p(T)=P(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$
The equation defines the adjoint notion without asserting existence. Existence and uniqueness for each admissible control are established under Countable Choice by [[lem-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-exists-uniquely]]. This sign convention is the one for the minimization Hamiltonian $H(t,x,p,u)=L(t,x,u)+p^T(A(t)x+B(t)u)$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $a\le b$.

1. If $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is absolutely continuous and $F'=0$ almost everywhere on $(a,b)$, then $F$ is constant.
2. Let $n\ge1$, let $y:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ have absolutely continuous coordinates, and let $h\in L^1([a,b];\mathbb R^n)$. If $y'_j=h_j$ almost everywhere for each coordinate $j$, then, for every $t\in[a,b]$,
$$y(t)=y(a)+\int_a^t h(s)\,ds.$$
Here $h\in L^1([a,b];\mathbb R^n)$ means that each coordinate $h_j$ is Lebesgue integrable, and the integral is the componentwise Lebesgue integral. For $a=b$ it is zero.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$.

1. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'$ extends
   continuously to $[a,b]$, then $f$ is Lipschitz.
2. Every Lipschitz $f$ is absolutely continuous.
3. Every absolutely continuous $f$ is continuous and has bounded variation.

Thus, with $C^1$ understood in the endpoint-extension sense of claim 1,
$C^1\subseteq\mathrm{Lipschitz}\subseteq AC\subseteq C\cap BV$ on a compact
interval.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $f$ is **bounded on $K$**: there is a real
$M \ge 0$ with

$$|f(x)| \le M \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, $f[K]$ is a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-bounded-set]]).

**The hypothesis is compactness of $K$, not of $A$**, and it cannot be relaxed
to boundedness of $K$ or to closedness of $K$ alone: the identity is unbounded
on the closed set $[0,\infty)$, and $x \mapsto 1/x$ is unbounded on the bounded
set $(0,1)$. The general statement of that is
[[thm-compactness-is-necessary-for-evt-and-uniform-continuity]], later on this
page.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

derivations.claim: The forcing $g(s):=Q(T-s)(x_u(T-s)-x_d(T-s))$ lies in $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^n)$: $Q$ is essentially bounded, $x_u$ is continuous on a compact interval and hence bounded, and $x_d\in L^2$. Also $C(s):=A(T-s)^T\in L^\infty$. Apply [F1] with $D(s)=I$ and initial value $q(0)=P(x_u(T)-x_T)$ to obtain an absolutely continuous $q$ satisfying the forward Volterra integral equation and $\dot q=Cq+g$ almost everywhere.

Set $p(t)=q(T-t)$. Time reversal preserves absolute continuity, and differentiating almost everywhere gives $-\dot p(t)=A(t)^Tp(t)+Q(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t))$ with $p(T)=q(0)=P(x_u(T)-x_T)$. Thus $p$ satisfies [F2].

If $\widetilde p$ is another adjoint solution, time reversal gives an absolutely continuous $\widetilde q(s)=\widetilde p(T-s)$ with $\widetilde q(0)=q(0)$ and $\dot{\widetilde q}=C\widetilde q+g$ almost everywhere. By [F4], $\widetilde q$ is continuous and bounded componentwise. Since $C\in L^\infty$, $g\in L^2$ and [F5] gives $g\in L^1$, the function $h=C\widetilde q+g$ belongs to $L^1$ componentwise. Apply [F3] to obtain $\widetilde q(s)=q(0)+\int_0^s(C(r)\widetilde q(r)+g(r))\,dr$ for every $s$. This is exactly the forward Volterra equation used to construct $q$ in step 1.1. Its actual integral-equation uniqueness in [F1] gives $\widetilde q=q$, hence $\widetilde p=p$.

The **ultrafilter extension principle** says that every filter on a set is contained in an ultrafilter on that set ([[def-ultrafilter]]).

It is also called the **ultrafilter lemma** and is equivalent over ZF to the Boolean prime ideal theorem, abbreviated BPI. Items below write **assume UL/BPI** precisely when they use this extension principle; they do not thereby assume the full axiom of choice.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. derivations.claim: By [F1], the state variation $\delta x=x_{u+w}-x$ is linear in $w$ and satisfies $\|\delta x\|_\infty\le C_0\|w\|_2$ for a fixed constant $C_0$. Expanding the running and terminal quadratic forms gives the linear term $\int_0^T (x-x_d)^TQ\delta x\,dt+\int_0^T u^TRw\,dt+(x(T)-x_T)^TP\delta x(T)$ and a remainder $\frac12\int_0^T(\delta x^TQ\delta x+w^TRw)dt+\frac12\delta x(T)^TP\delta x(T)$. Boundedness of $Q,R,P$ and the state-map estimate bound this remainder by $C\|w\|_2^2$. Thus the displayed linear term is the first-order norm derivative before rewriting its state contributions through the adjoint.

Apply [F3] to $p$ and $\delta x$, whose absolute continuity follows from [F1] and [F2]. Using their differential equations gives $p(T)^T\delta x(T)-p(0)^T\delta x(0)=-\int_0^T(x-x_d)^TQ\delta x\,dt+\int_0^T p^TBw\,dt$. Since $\delta x(0)=0$ and $p(T)=P(x(T)-x_T)$, rearranging yields $\int_0^T(x-x_d)^TQ\delta x\,dt+(x(T)-x_T)^TP\delta x(T)=\int_0^T p^TBw\,dt$.

Substitute the identity from step 1.2 into the derivative coefficient of step 1.1 and use $(p^TBw)=(B^Tp)^Tw$ and $(u^TRw)=(Ru)^Tw$ because $R=R^T$ almost everywhere. For a finite-dimensional real inner-product space $E$, a **cone** is a set closed under addition and multiplication by nonnegative scalars. A cone $K\subset E$ is **proper** when it is closed, convex, pointed ($K\cap(-K)=\{0\}$), and has nonempty interior. Its dual cone is
$$K^*=\{z\in E:\langle z,s\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }s\in K\}.$$

Let $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p$ and $G:\mathbb R^n\to E$ be linear, let $b\in\mathbb R^p$, $c\in\mathbb R^n$, and $h\in E$. A matrix $A$ has full row rank when its rows are linearly independent. The conic primal problem and its displayed dual pair are
$$\inf\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ h-Gx\in K\},\qquad \sup\{b^Ty-\langle h,z\rangle:A^Ty-G^*z=c,\ z\in K^*\},$$
where $G^*$ is the adjoint, defined by $\langle Gx,z\rangle=x^TG^*z$. For any feasible pair, its gap is
$$c^Tx-b^Ty+\langle h,z\rangle=\langle z,h-Gx\rangle\ge0.$$
The special case $\inf\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}$ has dual $\sup\{b^Ty:A^Ty+z=c,\ z\in K^*\}$ and gap $\langle z,x\rangle$.

For $K=\mathbb R_+^n$, the latter is the standard-form LP $\min c^Tx$ subject to $Ax=b$, $x\ge0$, with dual variables $y$ free and $s=c-A^Ty\ge0$. A convex QP in this convention has objective $f_0(x)=\tfrac12x^TQx+c^Tx$, with symmetric $Q\succeq0$, the same equality, and $x\ge0$. Its Lagrangian is $L(x,y,s)=f_0(x)+y^T(b-Ax)-s^Tx$; a feasible KKT tuple obeys $Qx+c-A^Ty-s=0$, and its dual value is $\inf_{w\in\mathbb R^n}L(w,y,s)$.

For a Lorentz cone $\mathcal L_{d+1}=\{(t,u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d:t\ge\|u\|_2\}$, let $F_j\in\mathbb R^{d_j\times n}$, $f_j\in\mathbb R^{d_j}$, $g_j\in\mathbb R^n$, and $h_j\in\mathbb R$. Then $\|F_jx+f_j\|_2\le g_j^Tx+h_j$ is membership of $(g_j^Tx+h_j,F_jx+f_j)$ in $\mathcal L_{d_j+1}$. With no equality constraints, the SOCP $\min c^Tx$ under these constraints has dual
$$\max -\sum_j(f_j^Tu_j+h_j\tau_j)\quad\text{subject to }\sum_j(F_j^Tu_j+g_j\tau_j)=c,\quad(\tau_j,u_j)\in\mathcal L_{d_j+1}.$$
For symmetric matrices, $S\succeq0$ means $v^TSv\ge0$ for every $v$ and the pairing is $\langle X,S\rangle=X\bullet S:=\operatorname{tr}(XS)$. Thus $\min C\bullet X$ subject to $\mathcal A(X)=b$, $X\succeq0$ has dual $\max b^Ty$ subject to $\mathcal A^*y+S=C$, $S\succeq0$, with gap $X\bullet S$. The affine-matrix SDP $\min c^Tx$ subject to $F_0+\sum_i x_iF_i\succeq0$ has dual $\max -F_0\bullet Z$ subject to $F_i\bullet Z=c_i$ for every $i$ and $Z\succeq0$.

The smooth convex inequality convention is that of [[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]: inequalities are written $g_i(x)\le0$ and their multipliers are nonnegative. The Lagrangian dual-value convention is that of [[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The smooth inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$
The critical cone for a KKT tuple is
$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

citations.quote: Assume the ultrafilter lemma, Dependent Choice, and Hahn–Banach. For the LQR data of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]], if the feasible-control set $\mathcal F$ is nonempty, convex, and weakly sequentially closed, then $J$ attains its minimum on $\mathcal F$ at a unique control $u^*$. The direct-method branch uses exactly these three principles; Dependent Choice also supplies Countable Choice for the $L^2$ Hilbert-space/reflexivity suppliers. No use of the full Axiom of Choice is asserted.

Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, state and control dimensions $n,m\ge1$, and the real quotient space $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$ of measurable controls modulo equality almost everywhere ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Let $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$ be equivalence classes, let $x_0,x_T\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $x_d\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^n)$. Let $U_c\subset\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, compact and convex. The pointwise control set is
$$
\mathcal U_c:=\{u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m):u(t)\in U_c\text{ for almost every }t\}.
$$
Let $Q\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $R\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{m\times m})$ be symmetric almost everywhere, with $Q(t)\succeq0$ and $rI\preceq R(t)\preceq MI$ almost everywhere for constants $0<r\le M<\infty$. Let $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite. For each $u\in\mathcal U_c$, its state is the unique continuous solution of the Volterra equation
$$
x_u(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x_u(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
The same state equation is defined for every $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and the running and terminal cost on that ambient space is
$$
J(u)=\frac12\int_0^T\!\left((x_u(t)-x_d(t))^TQ(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t))+u(t)^TR(t)u(t)\right)dt+\frac12(x_u(T)-x_T)^TP(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$
The constrained problem minimizes this ambient functional over $\mathcal F$, where additional path or terminal constraints are represented by a nonempty convex weakly sequentially closed set $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal U_c$; with no additional state constraints, $\mathcal F=\mathcal U_c$. “Weakly sequentially closed” means that every weakly convergent sequence in $\mathcal F$ has its weak limit in $\mathcal F$ ([[def-weak-convergence-of-nets-and-sequences]]). The definition asserts no optimizer or adjoint existence; the state-map well-definedness is supplied by [[lem-ctrl1-measurable-linear-ode-state-map]].

Let $U_c\subset\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, compact and convex, and let $\mathcal U_c$ be the pointwise admissible set in [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]]. If $u_k\in\mathcal U_c$ and $u_k\rightharpoonup u$ weakly in real $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, then $u\in\mathcal U_c$. Thus $\mathcal U_c$ is weakly sequentially closed.

Assume the ultrafilter lemma, DC and HB. Let $X$ be a real reflexive Banach space ([[def-reflexive-banach-space]]) and let $(u_j)$ be a norm-bounded sequence in $X$. Then $(u_j)$ has a subsequence converging weakly to a point of $X$ ([[def-weak-convergence-of-nets-and-sequences]]).
For the data of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]], if $u_k\in\mathcal U_c$ and $u_k\rightharpoonup u$ weakly in $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, then $J(u)\le\liminf_{k\to\infty}J(u_k)$.
For the data of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]], if $u_k,u\in\mathcal U_c$ and $u_k\rightharpoonup u$ weakly in $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, then $x_{u_k}\to x_u$ uniformly on $[0,T]$.

Let $T>0$, $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$, $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$, $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$. Write $\|A\|_\infty$ and $\|B\|_\infty$ for the essential suprema of their Euclidean operator norms. There is a unique absolutely continuous $x:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n$ satisfying
$$
x(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
Under Countable Choice it satisfies $\dot x=A x+B u$ almost everywhere, and it always satisfies
$$
\|x\|_\infty\le e^{\|A\|_\infty T}\left(\|x_0\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\sqrt T\,\|u\|_2\right).
$$
For fixed $A,B,x_0$, the map $u\mapsto x_u$ is affine into $C([0,T];\mathbb R^n)$, and its zero-initial-state linear part is bounded from $L^2$ to the supremum norm.

The almost-everywhere derivative assertion uses Countable Choice, as required by the cited $L^1$ fundamental theorem. The integral-equation existence, uniqueness, bound, and affine-map claims do not require that axiom.

The **ultrafilter extension principle** says that every filter on a set is contained in an ultrafilter on that set ([[def-ultrafilter]]).

It is also called the **ultrafilter lemma** and is equivalent over ZF to the Boolean prime ideal theorem, abbreviated BPI. Items below write **assume UL/BPI** precisely when they use this extension principle; they do not thereby assume the full axiom of choice.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every real or complex Hilbert space $H$ is reflexive: the canonical evaluation map $J_H:H\to H^{**}$ is surjective.

derivations.claim: Since $u_N\in\mathcal F_N\subseteq\mathcal U_c$ and $U_c$ is compact, $\sup_N\|u_N\|_2\le\sqrt T\sup_{c\in U_c}\|c\|_2<\infty$. Real $L^2$ is reflexive by [A1], so [F3] gives a weakly convergent subsequence from every subsequence of $(u_N)$.

Let a subsequence $u_{N_k}$ converge weakly to $\bar u$. Because each $u_{N_k}\in\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal F$ is weakly sequentially closed, $\bar u\in\mathcal F$. By [F4] and consistency, $J(\bar u)\le\liminf_kJ(u_{N_k})\le\limsup_k(J_{N_k}(u_{N_k})+\varepsilon_{N_k})$. Global discrete minimality gives $J_{N_k}(u_{N_k})\le J_{N_k}(v_{N_k})\le J(v_{N_k})+\varepsilon_{N_k}$. To see $J(v_{N_k})\to J(u^*)$, [F6] gives $\|x_{v_{N_k}}-x_{u^*}\|_\infty\le C\|v_{N_k}-u^*\|_2\to0$; the control quadratic difference is bounded by $\frac M2(\|v_{N_k}\|_2+\|u^*\|_2)\|v_{N_k}-u^*\|_2$, and state and terminal quadratic differences tend to zero by the corresponding bounded-quadratic estimate and uniform state convergence. Hence $J(v_{N_k})\to J(u^*)$, so $J(\bar u)\le J(u^*)$.

Since $\bar u\in\mathcal F$ and $u^*$ is the unique minimizer there, step 2.1 forces $\bar u=u^*$. Every subsequence therefore has a weakly convergent subsubsequence whose limit is $u^*$. If the full sequence failed to converge weakly to $u^*$, some bounded linear functional and some positive tolerance would witness failure along a subsequence; a weakly convergent subsubsequence from step 1.1 would contradict that witness. Thus $u_N\rightharpoonup u^*$.
Apply [F5] to the weakly convergent admissible controls from step 3.1 to obtain $x_{u_N}\to x_{u^*}$ uniformly on $[0,T]$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Assume the constraint set in [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]] is only the pointwise box $\mathcal F=\mathcal U_c$. For the uniform mesh $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$, $h=T/N$, define $P_Nu$ on $[t_j,t_{j+1})$ by $h^{-1}\int_{t_j}^{t_{j+1}}u(s)ds$. Then $P_Nu\in\mathcal U_c$ for every $u\in\mathcal U_c$, $P_Nu$ is piecewise constant, and $\|P_Nu-u\|_{L^2}\to0$ as $N\to\infty$. This recovery statement need not hold for additional state or terminal constraints unless they are separately shown to be preserved or approximated.

derivations.claim: Fix $v\in\mathcal F$ and put $d=v-u^*$. Convexity gives $u^*+\theta d\in\mathcal F$ for $0\le\theta\le1$. By [F2], $J(u^*+\theta d)-J(u^*)=\theta G_{u^*}[d]+\theta^2 R_d$, where $R_d=\tfrac12\int_0^T(\delta x_d^TQ\delta x_d+d^TRd)dt+\tfrac12\delta x_d(T)^TP\delta x_d(T)$. Minimality makes this expression nonnegative for $0<\theta\le1$; divide by $\theta$ and let $\theta\downarrow0$ to get $G_{u^*}[d]\ge0$. Also $R_d\ge\frac r2\|d\|_2^2$ since $Q,P\succeq0$ and $R\succeq rI$. Taking $\theta=1$ proves $J(v)-J(u^*)\ge\frac r2\|v-u^*\|_2^2$.

The assumed inequalities and consistency give $J(u_N)\le J_N(u_N)+\delta_N\le J_N(v_N)+\eta_N+\delta_N\le J(v_N)+\eta_N+2\delta_N\le J(u^*)+\rho_N+\eta_N+2\delta_N$. Subtract $J(u^*)$ and combine with step 1.1 to get the objective-gap bound.
Apply the growth inequality of step 1.1 at $v=u_N$. Substitute the upper objective-gap bound from step 2.1, divide by $r/2>0$, and take nonnegative square roots to obtain the control-error estimate.

For the stated sampled objective, subtract the quadrature of $\ell_w$ evaluated at the exact state. At every quadrature node, the state-cost difference is bounded by $\tfrac12\|Q\|_\infty(2E_N+e_N)e_N$; the control-cost summand is unchanged. Nonnegative weights with sum $T$ therefore bound the accumulated state perturbation by $\tfrac T2\|Q\|_\infty(2E_N+e_N)e_N$. The exact-state quadrature discrepancy is at most $q_N$. At $T$, the terminal quadratic difference is at most $\tfrac12\|P\|(2M_T+e_N)e_N$. Thus $|J_N(w)-J(w)|\le\delta_N$ for $w=u_N,v_N$ with the displayed $\delta_N$.

For any feasible $v$ with $\|v-u^*\|_2\le\sigma$, [F2] and [F3] bound the absolute difference of the state running terms by $\|Q\|_\infty E\sqrt T C_s\sigma$, the terminal terms by $\|P\|M_T C_s\sigma$, and the control terms by $M\sqrt T M_c\sigma$. Hence $J(v)-J(u^*)\le C_J\sigma$. Under [A1] the cell-average lemma gives strong recovery for the control-only case. If $u^*$ is $L_u$-Lipschitz, for each $t$ in a cell its distance from the cell average is at most $L_uh_N$, so $\|P_Nu^*-u^*\|_2\le\sqrt T L_uh_N$. Substitution gives the stated $\rho_N$ rate and completes the sufficient-estimate branch.

citations.quote:
**Inputs.** Supply pointwise smooth data on $[0,T]$ from [[def-ctrl1-smooth-transcription-data]], an original mesh, a piecewise-constant control parameterization, an explicit tableau from [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] or a possibly implicit tableau from [[def-ctrl1-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-collocation]], one of `single-shooting`, `multiple-shooting`, or `collocation` mode, a finite smooth representation of the control constraints when a solver-ready NLP is requested, finite sets of declared path-constraint times, endpoint constraints, the tableau quadrature rule, an initial decision vector $z_0$ and multiplier vector $\mu_0$, a stage residual tolerance $\tau_s\ge0$, a quadrature error tolerance $\tau_q\ge0$, a stage Newton correction cap $M_s\in\mathbb N_0$, and a maximum number of mesh nodes. Supply a deterministic derivative evaluator for the actual returned stage maps and resulting finite NLP on an open neighborhood of the queried candidate. On a locally fixed strict stopping branch of the finite stage-iteration procedure, differentiate that finite graph, including when the residual happens to be exactly zero at the queried point. Implicit differentiation as in [[thm-implicit-differentiation-forward-and-adjoint-formulas]] is permitted only when the selected returned stage map is certified to agree on that neighborhood with the exact local solution branch and its residual Jacobian is nonsingular there; an exact residual at the queried point alone does not establish this agreement. Return `derivative-failure` when no derivative of the actual returned map is available. Supply a quadrature error evaluator which returns a certified upper bound for the objective quadrature discrepancy or `unavailable`. Each supplied evaluator returns a value or failure in finite time. An optional trajectory-estimation request supplies the inputs of [[alg-bounded-adaptive-runge-kutta-controller]].
$$X_{j,i}=X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_{k<i}a_{ik}F_{j,k},\quad t_{j,i}=t_j+c_ih_j,\quad F_{j,i}=f(t_{j,i},X_{j,i},u_j),\quad \Phi_j(X_{j,0},u_j)=X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_i b_iF_{j,i}.$$

**Mesh and constraints.** Check $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$, all declared constraint and quadrature times in $[0,T]$, and all stage times $t_j+c_i h_j$ in $[0,T]$ before querying $f$ or $L$. An invalid time returns `mesh-domain-failure` with no evaluation. Insert every declared path-constraint time not already a node into the mesh, unless this exceeds the supplied node cap, in which case return `mesh-budget-exhausted`. Tie each inserted subcell's control to its original containing cell, so the parameterization is unchanged. A path constraint is evaluated at its declared times, now mesh nodes; an endpoint constraint is evaluated at its declared endpoint. This is finite sampling and does not assert continuous-path feasibility.

**Stage evaluation.** On each cell write $h_j=t_{j+1}-t_j$ and $u_j$ for its tied constant control. For an explicit tableau, form the stages recursively by the displayed equations. Before each query of $f$ or $L$, check that the time is in $[0,T]$, the state lies in $\Omega_x$, and the control lies in $\Omega_u$; a failed membership check returns `stage-domain-failure`, and an unavailable function value returns `stage-evaluation-failure` with the cell and stage index. Apply the same checks to every declared path-constraint evaluation.

For an implicit tableau, do not leave the collocation stages as outer NLP decision variables. Form the coupled slope residual
$$R_j(K;X_{j,0},u_j)_i=K_i-f\!\left(t_j+c_ih_j,X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_k a_{ik}K_k,u_j\right),\quad i=1,\ldots,s.$$
Its open domain consists of stage vectors for which every state-control input is in the smooth-data tube. In the sampled linear-quadratic branch, form the finite matrix $M_j$ with blocks $(M_j)_{ik}=\delta_{ik}I-h_ja_{ik}A(t_{j,i})$ and right-hand side $r_i=A(t_{j,i})X_{j,0}+B(t_{j,i})u_j$. Use exact Gaussian elimination on the stored sample coefficients: scan columns left to right, pivot on the first nonzero entry at or below the current row, swap, eliminate below, and back-substitute. If no pivot is available, return `singular-stage-matrix`; otherwise the exact solution of $M_jK=r$ is the stage vector and the nonlinear-solve status is `exact-linear-stage-solve`. In all other smooth cases, form the deterministic initial guess $K_i^{(0)}=f(t_j,X_{j,0},u_j)$ after checking that this query is defined. Before calling Newton, check that the entire seed $K^{(0)}$ belongs to the declared open domain of $R_j$, equivalently that every induced stage state lies in $\Omega_x$ and every required control lies in $\Omega_u$. If this check fails, return `stage-domain-failure` with the failing cell and stage index, the partial result record, and no objective candidate. Otherwise call [[alg-finite-budget-newton-for-vector-residuals]] on $R_j$ with that open evaluation domain, tolerance $\tau_s$ and cap $M_s$. Record its iterate, residual vector, and exact status for each cell. Only `root` supplies a stage candidate; it means $\|R_j\|_2\le\tau_s$, not an exact root unless $\tau_s=0$. Any other status returns the partial result record with `nlp_status=stage-solve-failure`, the failing cell, and no objective candidate. On a returned stage vector use $X_{j,i}=X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_k a_{ik}K_k$ and $\Phi_j=X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_i b_iK_i$. A singular stage Jacobian or failed stage query is reported, not interpreted as lack of an exact solution.

**Transcription modes.** In single shooting, the decision variables are the original-cell controls; set $X_{0,0}=x_0$ and recursively compute $X_{j+1,0}=\Phi_j(X_{j,0},u_j)$. In multiple shooting, the decision variables are node states and controls; fix $X_{0,0}=x_0$ and define defects $d_j=X_{j+1,0}-\Phi_j(X_{j,0},u_j)$. In collocation mode, use the same node/control variables and solved internal stage states; the collocation equations are solved internally by the implicit-stage procedure above. Explicit stages are likewise internal deterministic evaluations. In every mode the finite feasible set includes $u_j\in U_c$ for each original cell. The finite objective is $\sum_j h_j\sum_i b_iL(t_{j,i},X_{j,i},u_j)+\phi(X_{N,0})$, and the finite constraints are exactly the declared node/time constraints, the represented control constraints, and endpoint constraints. If $U_c$ is available only as a compact set-membership constraint and has no finite smooth representation, return the finite set-constrained model with `nlp_status=not-smooth-nlp`; the dispatcher must not treat it as an SQP-ready NLP. A QP solver route additionally requires the sampled control constraints to be affine.

**Output.** Evaluate the supplied initial candidate and return a record containing its ordered decision variables, defect residuals, per-cell implicit-stage residuals, path/endpoint constraint residuals, KKT residuals, and objective value, when available. For equality residual $h$, inequality residual $g\le0$, and multiplier pair $(\nu,\lambda)$, report $r_p=(h,[g]_+)$, $r_d=\nabla J_N+Dh^T\nu+Dg^T\lambda$, $r_\lambda=[-\lambda]_+$, and $r_c=\lambda\odot g$. Include a model that can reevaluate these quantities at a later solver candidate. Return separate `nlp_status`, per-cell `implicit_stage_status`, optional `ivp_status`, `quadrature_status`, `mesh_status`, and `budget_status` fields. A quadrature bound at most $\tau_q$ is `bound-met`; a larger bound is `bound-not-met`; an unavailable bound is `unavailable`. The build-stage budget field is `not-run`; the solver dispatcher fills its final value. A failed derivative evaluation leaves KKT residuals unavailable with its exact status. An unevaluated optional IVP estimate is `not-requested`; if requested, report the adaptive controller's exact finite status, not an error certificate.

This direct transcription samples pointwise data; an $L^\infty$ equivalence class without a chosen representative and sampling rule is not stage-evaluable. For a single-shooting reduced objective represented as the finite state-step graph of [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]], its exact real-arithmetic reduced gradient is given by [[thm-discrete-adjoint-gradient-recursion]]. Agreement with the continuous ODE adjoint gradient is only conditional on the weighted discrete-gradient representation and the separate state, adjoint, derivative-data, endpoint, and quadrature estimates in [[thm-discrete-continuous-gradient-error-order-p]]. The optional adaptive RK estimate is separate from the fixed NLP and its embedded difference is not a certified global error bound. The algorithm makes no continuous-path feasibility, convergence-rate, global-optimality, or unconditioned discrete-adjoint accuracy claim.

For pointwise numerical transcription on $[0,T]$, the data consist of an integer $n\ge1$, open sets $\Omega_x\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $\Omega_u\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a nonempty compact convex control set $U_c\subset\Omega_u$, an initial state $x_0\in\Omega_x$, a pointwise-defined vector field $f:[0,T]\times\Omega_x\times\Omega_u\to\mathbb R^n$, a pointwise-defined running cost $L:[0,T]\times\Omega_x\times\Omega_u\to\mathbb R$, and a terminal cost $\phi:\Omega_x\to\mathbb R$. The admissible state solves $\dot x(t)=f(t,x(t),u(t))$ almost everywhere and the continuous objective is $\int_0^T L(t,x(t),u(t))dt+\phi(x(T))$. Optional path and endpoint constraints are pointwise-defined functions evaluated at declared continuous times or transcription nodes. A **compact tube** is a compact subset of $[0,T]\times\Omega_x\times\Omega_u$ containing the state/control triples used by stages and trajectories. On such a tube, $f,L,\phi$ and any constraint functions used in a local NLP theorem are continuous and have continuous state/control derivatives through order three (the $C^3$ convention of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), with those derivatives bounded. An $L^\infty$ equivalence class alone has no specified value at a Runge–Kutta stage time, so it is not an admissible stage-evaluation input without an additional pointwise representative and sampling rule. This definition makes no existence, convergence, or continuous-path-feasibility claim.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The smooth inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$
The critical cone for a KKT tuple is
$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $x_*$ be a KKT point of a $C^2$ nonlinear program, with multiplier
$\mu_*=(\nu_*,\lambda_{*,I})$ and active set $I=I(x_*)$. Assume LICQ,
strict complementarity $\lambda_{*,i}>0$ for every $i\in I$, and the
second-order sufficient condition
$$d^T\nabla^2_{xx}L(x_*,\mu_*)d>0 \quad\text{for every nonzero critical direction }d.$$
Assume also that the active KKT map $F_A$ has a locally Lipschitz
Jacobian: on some ball, $\|DF_A(z)-DF_A(z\prime)\|_2\le L\|z-z\prime\|_2$.
Once the correct active set is used, exact arithmetic full steps of
[[alg-sqp-exact-hessian-newton-step]], started sufficiently close to
$(x_*,\mu_*)$, are well-defined and converge quadratically to that pair.
This is the local full-step Newton result; it does not assert acceptance by
an L1 merit line search.

For the $C^2$ program of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]], suppose $x_*$ is
feasible and has KKT multipliers $(\nu,\lambda)$. If
$$
d^T\nabla_{xx}^2L(x_*,\nu,\lambda)d>0\quad\text{for every nonzero }d\in\mathcal K(x_*,\nu,\lambda),
$$
then $x_*$ is a strict local minimizer. The condition is vacuous when the
critical cone is $\{0\}$; no constraint qualification is assumed.

Let $x_*$ be a KKT point of a $C^2$ nonlinear program, with multiplier
$\mu_*=(\nu_*,\lambda_{*,I})$ and active set $I=I(x_*)$. Assume LICQ,
strict complementarity $\lambda_{*,i}>0$ for every $i\in I$, and the
second-order sufficient condition
$$d^T\nabla^2_{xx}L(x_*,\mu_*)d>0 \quad\text{for every nonzero critical direction }d.$$
Assume also that the active KKT map $F_A$ has a locally Lipschitz
Jacobian: on some ball, $\|DF_A(z)-DF_A(z\prime)\|_2\le L\|z-z\prime\|_2$.
Once the correct active set is used, exact arithmetic full steps of
[[alg-sqp-exact-hessian-newton-step]], started sufficiently close to
$(x_*,\mu_*)$, are well-defined and converge quadratically to that pair.
This is the local full-step Newton result; it does not assert acceptance by
an L1 merit line search.

derivations.claim: A fixed transcription has finitely many decision variables. By the regularity hypothesis in the Statement and [F1], its actual objective and constraint functions have continuous derivatives through order three on a neighborhood of the KKT point. For an implicit-stage transcription this hypothesis includes the selected local stage-solve branch; no differentiability of that branch is inferred from the smooth-data definition alone.

The KKT map for the identified active set is built from the first derivatives of those objective and constraint functions. Its Jacobian is locally Lipschitz by continuity and local boundedness of their third derivatives in [F5]. The assumed LICQ, strict complementarity, and SOSC from [F4] are exactly the remaining hypotheses of [F3].

Apply [F3] to the active KKT system. It provides a neighborhood in which exact-Hessian full Newton steps are defined and converge quadratically from a sufficiently close start, which is the asserted fixed-mesh branch. The dispatcher has a finite outer cap, so it can stop before the local sequence converges.

For the mesh-family branch, set $A_N=D\mathcal K_N(z_N^0)$ and $T_N(z)=z-A_N^{-1}\mathcal K_N(z)$. If $\varepsilon_N=0$, $z_N^0$ is already a root. Otherwise take the closed ball of radius $R_N=2\beta\varepsilon_N$. The residual bound gives $\|T_N(z_N^0)-z_N^0\|\le\beta\varepsilon_N=R_N/2$. For $z$ in that ball, the uniform Lipschitz bound gives $\|DT_N(z)\|=\|I-A_N^{-1}D\mathcal K_N(z)\|\le\beta L R_N\le1/2$. Thus $T_N$ maps the ball into itself and is a contraction. Completeness [F7] gives its unique fixed point $z_N^*$, which is exactly the unique root of $\mathcal K_N$ there and satisfies $\|z_N^*-z_N^0\|\le R_N$.

By boundedness of $E_N$, $\|E_Nz_N^*-z^\dagger\|_Z\le C_E\|z_N^*-z_N^0\|+\|E_Nz_N^0-z^\dagger\|_Z\le2C_E\beta\varepsilon_N+\|E_Nz_N^0-z^\dagger\|_Z$, which tends to zero. The assumed LICQ, strict complementarity, SOSC, local Lipschitz conditions, and common basin let [F6] apply at each $z_N^*$; hence each exact-Hessian full-step sequence from that basin converges quadratically.

citations.quote:
Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, state and control dimensions $n,m\ge1$, and the real quotient space $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$ of measurable controls modulo equality almost everywhere ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Let $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$ be equivalence classes, let $x_0,x_T\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $x_d\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^n)$. Let $U_c\subset\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, compact and convex. The pointwise control set is
$$
\mathcal U_c:=\{u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m):u(t)\in U_c\text{ for almost every }t\}.
$$
Let $Q\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $R\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{m\times m})$ be symmetric almost everywhere, with $Q(t)\succeq0$ and $rI\preceq R(t)\preceq MI$ almost everywhere for constants $0<r\le M<\infty$. Let $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite. For each $u\in\mathcal U_c$, its state is the unique continuous solution of the Volterra equation
$$
x_u(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x_u(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
The same state equation is defined for every $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and the running and terminal cost on that ambient space is
$$
J(u)=\frac12\int_0^T\!\left((x_u(t)-x_d(t))^TQ(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t))+u(t)^TR(t)u(t)\right)dt+\frac12(x_u(T)-x_T)^TP(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$
The constrained problem minimizes this ambient functional over $\mathcal F$, where additional path or terminal constraints are represented by a nonempty convex weakly sequentially closed set $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal U_c$; with no additional state constraints, $\mathcal F=\mathcal U_c$. “Weakly sequentially closed” means that every weakly convergent sequence in $\mathcal F$ has its weak limit in $\mathcal F$ ([[def-weak-convergence-of-nets-and-sequences]]). The definition asserts no optimizer or adjoint existence; the state-map well-definedness is supplied by [[lem-ctrl1-measurable-linear-ode-state-map]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

For every LQR data set in [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]] and every admissible control $u$, the adjoint in [[def-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-equation]] exists and is unique.

For the data of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]] and an admissible control $u$ with state $x_u$, a **continuous LQR adjoint** is an absolutely continuous curve $p:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n$ satisfying, almost everywhere,
$$
-\dot p(t)=A(t)^Tp(t)+Q(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t)),\qquad p(T)=P(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$
The equation defines the adjoint notion without asserting existence. Existence and uniqueness for each admissible control are established under Countable Choice by [[lem-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-exists-uniquely]]. This sign convention is the one for the minimization Hamiltonian $H(t,x,p,u)=L(t,x,u)+p^T(A(t)x+B(t)u)$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice.

For the LQR problem of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]], let $u\in\mathcal U_c$, let $x=x_u$, and let $p$ be its adjoint from [[def-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-equation]]. Define the bounded linear map $DJ(u):L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)\to\mathbb R$ by
$$DJ(u)[w]=\int_0^T\big(B(t)^Tp(t)+R(t)u(t)\big)^Tw(t)\,dt.$$
It is the first-order norm derivative of $J$ at $u$ in the precise sense that $J(u+w)-J(u)-DJ(u)[w]=O(\|w\|_2^2)$ as $\|w\|_2\to0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Put $m=\int_0^1u(t)dt$. Since $\int_0^1(u-m)^2dt=\int_0^1u^2dt-m^2$, direct expansion gives $J(u)=\frac12\|u-m\|_2^2+\frac12[m^2+(m-1)^2]=\frac12\|u-m\|_2^2+(m-\frac12)^2+\frac14$.

Both squared terms are nonnegative, so $J(u)\ge\frac14$. Equality holds exactly when $u=m$ almost everywhere and $m=\frac12$, hence exactly for $u^*(t)=\frac12$ almost everywhere. This control satisfies $[-1,1]$ and direct substitution gives $J(u^*)=\frac14$. Therefore it is the unique minimizer.

The state is $x(t)=t/2$. By [F2], the adjoint equation is $-\dot p=0$ with terminal value $p(1)=x(1)-1=-1/2$. The constant curve $p(t)=-1/2$ solves it, and uniqueness in [F2] makes this the adjoint. Under [A1], [F3] gives the reduced gradient $g=p+u^*=0$. Thus $g(t)(c-u^*(t))=0$ for every $c\in[-1,1]$, so the control-only pointwise variational inequality holds with equality for this example.
